title: Quantum stochastic thermodynamics of macroscopic systems: an algebraic approach
abstract: We build a framework for the thermodynamics of macroscopic quantum systems. In contrast with approaches requiring access to the full density matrix, our framework relies on a coarse-grained description, based on measurement statistics of a few observables. When these observables commute, the outcomes define classical macrostates whose entropy is quantified by observational entropy, accounting for uncertainty about both the macrostate and the microstate within it. We extend this notion to non-commuting observables forming a subalgebra of the operator space, and use Jaynes' principle to define an algebra-dependent entropy interpolating between von Neumann and observational entropies. Given initial and final measurement sets, connected by internal and/or environment-induced dynamics, we derive a second law for the coarse-grained dynamics. Unlike formulations based on von Neumann entropy, our inequality captures irreversibility from both non-unitary environment-induced dynamics and internal equilibration. It takes the usual form of a positive entropy production when the system is initially at internal equilibrium, while correction terms capture nonequilibrium resources ignored by the coarse-graining. We also derive fluctuation theorems for coarse-grained thermodynamic quantities. Along a quasi-static path of measurement schemes, we identify quantum macroscopic notions of work and heat fulfilling the first and second laws, including an additional work contribution from manipulating the algebra to which the system is confined, through external constraints or quantum measurement backaction. Finally, we apply our framework to examples illustrating the impact of varying the coarse-graining scheme. Our approach unifies macroscopic and stochastic thermodynamics in a genuinely quantum framework, laying the basis for a versatile, experimentally friendly toolbox to analyze complex quantum dynamics.
summary: This paper introduces an algebraic framework for quantum stochastic thermodynamics that bypasses the need to track the full system density matrix. By focusing only on measurable observables, it defines a generalized entropy that interpolates between microscopic and macroscopic descriptions. The resulting formalism yields fundamental thermodynamic laws, including fluctuation theorems and novel work contributions from measurement backaction.
main_problem: To develop a quantum thermodynamic framework capable of describing macroscopic systems by bridging the gap between fine-grained stochastic dynamics and macroscopic equilibrium thermodynamics.
main_result: The authors derive a generalized second law for coarse-grained dynamics that captures irreversibility from both environment interaction and internal equilibration, while also identifying an additional work term related to manipulating the system's measurement algebra.
method: The approach utilizes a coarse-graining formalism based on measuring only a limited set of observables (forming an accessible subalgebra), defining entropy via Jaynes' principle for this reduced description.
model_or_system: The framework applies to general macroscopic quantum systems undergoing internal or environment-induced dynamics, considering both open-system and autonomous system viewpoints.
key_observables: Observational entropy, algebra-dependent entropy, work, heat, and the generalized entropy production rate.
important_parameters: The nature of the coarse-graining observable set (commuting vs. non-commuting) and the path taken between initial and final measurement schemes.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the system's dynamics can be effectively described by restricting attention to an accessible subalgebra of observables, thereby circumventing the need for the full density matrix.

paper_structure: The paper builds conceptually by first defining the coarse-grained entropy (especially in the commutative case), then deriving the second law and fluctuation theorems, followed by introducing work and heat increments via quasi-static transformations, and finally extending the formalism to general non-commutative observable algebras.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant as it provides a rigorous, algebraically grounded method for defining thermodynamic quantities (work, heat) in open quantum systems where full state knowledge is impossible, directly impacting research in quantum thermodynamics and measurement theory.
